# The baselines, and what a fair comparison means {#sec-baselines}

**ISLA is measured against the two released slice-attention transformers
with the strongest record on industrial aerodynamics, GeoTransolver and
Transolver, under one protocol that fixes everything except the
architecture.** The baselines are strong, not straw: GeoTransolver has at
least as many parameters as ISLA and receives raw coordinates that ISLA
never sees; both are run at their own best learning rate; neither is ever
modified. This chapter says what each baseline computes and sees, states the
protocol as a list of rules, and settles three questions the evidence
chapters would otherwise have to carry: why every model must receive the
freestream as a unit direction, why ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract
rather than an accuracy advantage over a canonicalized baseline, and why the
learning rate belongs to the protocol.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's routing mechanism and differ in
what they are allowed to see: raw coordinates in a frame, and the freestream
as a raw vector.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture: *physics attention*. GeoTransolver adds a
geometry encoder and a global-context projector. @fig-family-diagram places
ISLA beside them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-family-diagram
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   What each architecture is handed, and where they differ. Grey boxes
%%|   are data; the routing mechanism (solid blue) is shared by the whole
%%|   family. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive coordinates in the
%%|   dataset's frame and the freestream as a vector; ISLA receives only
%%|   invariants of the same inputs and its slices carry the surface measure
%%|   (dashed blue: fixed maps with no parameters). How to read this: the
%%|   diagram shows inputs and structure, not accuracy; the learned blocks are
%%|   the same kind of object in all three.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph B["GeoTransolver / Transolver"]
        direction TB
        B1["per point: centred coordinates, unit normal<br/>global: freestream vector (unit direction under the protocol)"]:::data
        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>global-context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: pressure, wall shear"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction TB
        I1["per point: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["invariant seed; length scale from the total measure"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["linear head on invariants → equivariant basis"]:::fixed
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
    end
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface
point it receives the coordinates, centred on the case, and the unit normal
as a six-channel feature; the freestream vector is a three-channel global
feature. Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through
a dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the
ball-query local-feature path is off throughout this program. It is not
rotation- or translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different
input (@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the freestream vector is broadcast to every point.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and measure weight per point and the
freestream as a unit direction, consumed only through invariants and
equivariant anchors (@sec-mt2). @tbl-architectures gives the three
configurations side by side.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices | parameters | peak memory at 10,000 tokens |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centred coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | freestream vector through the global-context projector: the unit direction under the protocol | 12 | 256 | 256 | 9.0M | 2.70 GiB |
| Transolver | centred coordinates, unit normal | freestream vector, broadcast per point: the unit direction under the protocol | 8 | 256 | 256 | 6.0M | not measured |
| ISLA (reference configuration) | position, unit normal, measure weight, through invariants and anchors only | unit freestream direction | 12 | 192 | 256 | 8.9M | 1.30 GiB with the geometry recompute; 1.94 GiB without |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 10,000 sampled surface cells per
case. *Layers*: soft-slice attention blocks. *Hidden*: width of the per-point
feature. *Parameters*: trainable parameters of the recipe configuration.
*Peak memory*: peak allocated GPU memory over one training step on one case
of 10,000 cells in bfloat16 on one GB300, both models compiled as the recipe
runs them (results/kernel_study_2026-09-13/pareto_gb300_full_bf16.json;
@sec-mt2-cost); not measured for Transolver, which serves as a same-family
control. Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

### The freestream must enter as a unit direction

**The numerical scale at which the baselines receive the freestream is a
protocol variable, and on HiLiftAeroML it moves their error more than any
architectural choice in this book.** ISLA normalizes its global vector
inputs by construction. GeoTransolver and Transolver consume whatever vector
the pipeline hands them, and the dataset pipelines pass the physical
freestream velocity through without normalizing: 2,679.5 in/s on
HiLiftAeroML (the dataset is in inches and seconds) and 38.9 m/s on
DrivAerML. Coordinates and fields are nondimensionalized; this one vector is
not.

Why it matters is visible before training. GeoTransolver's global-context
projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the vector directly, so
its conditioning depends on the magnitude: @tbl-projector shows how many
slices each head of the untrained projector occupies as the magnitude
grows. At unit magnitude a head spreads over most of the 256 slices; at the
HiLiftAeroML magnitude it collapses onto one. Transolver concatenates the raw
vector into every point's features, with the same hazard in a different
place. Training can in principle rescale either path, so these numbers are
the initialization signature; the trained measurement is what counts.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-projector
#| output: asis
cond = J("geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json")["results"]
out = "| magnitude of the freestream vector | occupied slices per head (entropy-equivalent, min to max over heads) | largest context entry |\n|---:|---|---:|\n"
labels = {1.0: "1 (unit direction)", 38.9: "38.9 (DrivAerML, m/s)", 2679.5054741899685: "2,679.5 (HiLiftAeroML, in/s)"}
for r in cond:
    lab = next(v for k, v in labels.items() if abs(k - r["drive_magnitude"]) < 1e-6)
    out += f"| {lab} | {r['effective_slices_min']:.1f} to {r['effective_slices_max']:.1f} of 256 | {r['context_abs_max']:.2f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Conditioning of GeoTransolver's global-context projector at initialization against the magnitude of the "
      "freestream vector it receives, at the recipe's projector dimensions with untrained weights. "
      "How to read this: a head that occupies one slice has lost its ability to condition on the direction; "
      "this is a property of the untrained network, and @tbl-unit-vs-physical is the trained consequence. "
      "Data: results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-projector}")
```

The trained consequence, at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same
cases, seeds and budget in both arms, is in @tbl-unit-vs-physical: each
baseline fed the unit direction is more accurate than its physical-velocity
twin on every one of the 180 validation cases, by a median factor above
three, and the unit-direction baselines are ahead of ISLA's reference
configuration.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unit-vs-physical
#| output: asis
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
rf = J("relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json")["hilift_val"]
ud = J("udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json")["paired"]
fp = lambda keys: [fp35[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver, physical velocity, lr 1e-3", fp([f"lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 1e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3 (its best at this rung)", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])),
    ("Transolver, physical velocity, lr 3e-3", fp([f"t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("Transolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("ISLA, reference configuration", [rf[f"rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]),
]
isla_ref = mean(arms[5][1])
out = "| arm | surface pressure error, seed mean (seeds) | baseline ÷ ISLA reference |\n|---|---|---:|\n"
for lab, v in arms:
    ratio = "—" if lab.startswith("ISLA") else f"{mean(v)/isla_ref:.2f}"
    out += f"| {lab} | {mean(v):.4f} ({' / '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in v)}) | {ratio} |\n"
print(out)
g, t = ud["gt_physical_35_vs_gt_unit_35"], ud["transolver_physical_35_vs_transolver_unit_35"]
print(f": The input-scale control at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure "
      f"on the 180 shared validation cases, float32, final-epoch checkpoints, 10,000 cells, 500 epochs. Paired per case, "
      f"the unit-direction GeoTransolver is lower than its physical-velocity twin on {g['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of "
      f"{g['n_cases']} cases (median factor {g['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}) and the unit-direction Transolver on "
      f"{t['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of {t['n_cases']} (median factor {t['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}). "
      f"How to read this: the physical-velocity rows measure an input scale, not an architecture, and appear nowhere else in "
      f"the book as a comparison; the unit-direction rows are the protocol. Data: "
      f"results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json, results/relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json, "
      f"results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (paired counts). {{#tbl-unit-vs-physical}}")
```

Three rules follow. Every architecture receives the freestream as a unit
direction, and a comparison against a baseline fed the physical velocity is
reported only as a measurement of the input scale. The unit-direction
baseline is the reference baseline on every rung. And the input scale is
fixed by rule rather than by control: learning-rate, training-length and
seed controls vary the optimizer and cannot detect an input-scale defect.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the hazard is small: DrivAerML and the interior task"}
At the DrivAerML magnitude the projector's collapse at initialization is
partial (@tbl-projector), and the trained effect is nil: GeoTransolver
trained on the physical velocity and on the unit direction score within a
percent of each other at 435 cars (@sec-full-data). GeoTransolver's volume
configuration on the interior task changes by under 2% on every field
between the two inputs (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), so the interior ordering
is not an input-scale effect. The rule is applied on every dataset
regardless, because a rule that depends on the dataset's units is not a
rule.
:::

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book was produced under the
following rules; a comparison that violates one is not reported.** The
datasets and splits are in @sec-splits, the metric in @sec-metrics and the
training recipe in @sec-protocol.

1. **Matched tokens per case: 10,000 sampled surface cells for every
   architecture.** Accuracy still rises with tokens at 10,000
   (@tbl-token-control), so a token mismatch would be a handicap disguised as
   an architecture difference.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm.** Doubling GeoTransolver's budget at
   the small rungs does not lower its error (@sec-data-efficiency), so 500
   does not under-train the baseline.
3. **Learning rate chosen per architecture on the full split, by validation,
   before any ladder or ablation ran, then frozen.** Where a baseline had no
   full-split run on a dataset it was trained at both grid rates on the
   small rungs and is reported at the better, a choice that favours the
   baseline (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives the freestream as the unit direction**
   (@sec-part-baseline).
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually**, so the reader can
   see whether a ratio exceeds the seed spread.
6. **Shared validation cases**, sampled with the same seed, for every
   architecture.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed**: the count of
   validation cases on which one architecture is more accurate, with median
   and worst-decile per-case ratios, alongside the ratio of means.
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once**, taken verbatim from the dataset
   manifest; sealed per checkpoint, not per program (@sec-splits).
9. **Preregistered bars**: each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and evaluation
configuration: on DrivAerML, surface pressure and wall shear on 48 held-out
cars at 10,000 sampled cells; on HiLiftAeroML, pressure, velocity and wall
shear on 180 held-out cases shared by every training split. An instrument is
never widened after a result is read from it; a control that changes it
(another cell count, a rotated pose, a biased sampling density) is reported
as such and never mixed into an in-family number. Its limits bind where
stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and two seeds a thin noise
estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**At the recipe operating point ISLA matches GeoTransolver on parameters
and tokens per case, and on the compiled path it matches on step time at
half the memory.** Parameters 8.9M against 9.0M; tokens per case 10,000
each; on one GB300 in bfloat16 with both models compiled as the recipe runs
them, ISLA's step is 1.05x GeoTransolver's at 10,000 tokens with the
geometry recompute on and 0.86x with it off, at 1.30 and 1.94 GiB against
2.70 GiB (@tbl-mt2-cost). Memory was not a controlled variable in any
comparison and no accuracy result depends on it: the checkpoints in this
book were trained by implementations of the same function that differ only
in footprint.

@tbl-token-control is the token-count control behind rule 1. It compares
ISLA against itself at two cell counts, at one shared learning rate that is
not ISLA's best; it was run on the legacy centred variant (diagnostic), a
within-model control whose reading does not depend on the frame. The 8% it
shows is the price of fewer sampled points per case, and the reason the
protocol fixes tokens for every architecture.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-token-control
#| output: asis
iw = J("instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json")
p = lambda k: iw[k]["pressure_l2"]
mt2_const_10k = [p(f"ref_mt2_v3c_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
mt2_const_6500 = [p(f"iw_mt2_v3c_r6500_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
gt_10k = [p(f"ref_gt_fixed_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
ratio = mean(mt2_const_6500) / mean(mt2_const_10k)
rows = [("ISLA, legacy centred variant (diagnostic)", "10,000", mt2_const_10k, 1.0),
        ("ISLA, legacy centred variant (diagnostic)", "6,500", mt2_const_6500, ratio),
        ("GeoTransolver", "10,000", gt_10k, None)]
out = "| architecture | tokens per case | surface pressure error (seed 42 / 43) | relative to ISLA at 10,000 |\n|---|--:|---|--:|\n"
for n, t, v, r in rows:
    out += f"| {n} | {t} | {v[0]:.4f} / {v[1]:.4f} | {'—' if r is None else f'{r:.2f}x'} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The token-count control on DrivAerML: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure, mean over the 48 "
      "validation cars, scored in bfloat16 (labelled: this table predates the float32 instrument and compares ISLA "
      "with itself), at learning rate 3e-3 for every row. The last column divides the row's seed mean by that of ISLA "
      "at 10,000 tokens. How to read this: a token-count control, not a matched-memory comparison, and a within-model "
      "control run on the legacy centred variant, so its reading is the token count's, not the frame's; wall shear moves the "
      "same way. Data: results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json. {#tbl-token-control}")
```

## Pose: equivariant by construction, invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**ISLA is rotation- and translation-covariant by algebraic construction;
GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at
about a percent of accuracy cost. Against a canonicalized baseline the two
are equally good, so equivariance is a contract about what the model needs
at inference, not an accuracy advantage.** Against baselines that learn pose
from rotation augmentation instead, ISLA leads when every car arrives in a
random pose (@sec-scoreboard-pose; that measurement was made on the legacy
centred variant, and the reference configuration's re-measurement is
running, @sec-nb-refprops-prereg).

The two phrases mean different things. A model is *equivariant by
construction* when every operation inside it commutes with rigid motions, so
a rotated case yields the rotated prediction to roundoff (ISLA's float64
contract test, @sec-mt2-contracts). A pipeline is *invariant by
canonicalization* when a preprocessing step estimates a frame from each
case, expresses the case in that frame, runs an ordinary model, and rotates
vector outputs back; it is invariant exactly when the frame estimate depends
on the pose-free geometry alone. The canonical frame used here sends the
freestream direction to +x and fixes the roll about it from the
area-weighted principal axes of the surface in the transverse plane, sign
from the third moment. @tbl-pose measures GeoTransolver on DrivAerML under
three treatments, *in pose* (cars as the dataset provides them) and on an
*SO(3) orbit* (each car in a uniformly random orientation), with vector
outputs rotated back before scoring.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pose
#| output: asis
p1 = J("p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json")
pp = J("p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json")
raw_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
raw_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_in = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_orb = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["orbit_SO3_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
ref = mean(raw_in)
orbit_ratios = [v / p1["prior"]["gt_inpose_pressure_l2"] for v in p1["prior"]["gt_p1_orbit_pressure_l2"].values()]
fx = lambda r: f"{r:.0f}x" if r >= 10 else f"{r:.2f}x"
def row(name, a, b):
    return f"| {name} | {a[0]:.4f} / {a[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(a)/ref)}) | {b[0]:.4f} / {b[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(b)/ref)}) |\n"
out = "| GeoTransolver treatment | in pose (seed 42 / 43) | SO(3) orbit (seed 42 / 43) |\n|---|---|---|\n"
out += row("trained and evaluated in the recipe frame", raw_in, raw_orb)
out += row("trained in the recipe frame, canonicalized at inference only", eval_canon_in, eval_canon_orb)
out += row("trained and evaluated in the canonical frame", tr_in, tr_orb)
print(out)
print(f": Pose dependence of GeoTransolver on DrivAerML: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure over the 48 "
      f"validation cars, learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs, seed 42 / seed 43, scored in bfloat16 (labelled: these runs "
      f"predate the float32 instrument and are used only for within-architecture pose factors); the parenthesized factor divides the seed "
      f"mean by the in-pose seed mean of the first row ({ref:.4f}). Across three seeds of the recipe-frame model the "
      f"orbit penalty spans {min(orbit_ratios):.0f} to {max(orbit_ratios):.0f}x. How to read this: ISLA is not shown "
      f"because its orbit and in-pose predictions agree to roundoff by construction; wall shear behaves the same way. "
      f"Data: results/p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json (rows 1 and 2), "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json (row 3). {{#tbl-pose}}")
```

Three things follow. GeoTransolver in the recipe frame is not pose-robust: a
random orientation multiplies its error by more than twenty. Canonicalization
must be in the training pipeline: applied only at inference to a model
trained in one exact pose it is pose-invariant but costs 1.6 to 1.7x,
because that model is hypersensitive to the sub-degree tilt of the frame
estimate, and a model that sees the estimator's tilt noise during training
learns to ignore it (third row). And on this data ISLA's exact equivariance
and canonicalized GeoTransolver deliver the same pose invariance, so no
accuracy claim in this book is attributed to equivariance; the pose contract
is scored as a contract.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What the contract still buys"}
Canonicalization needs a known global direction at inference and a
principal frame whose sign can be resolved; both hold for every vehicle and
wing here (no DrivAerML case is within 5% of a principal-axis degeneracy).
They fail for a PDE surrogate with no distinguished global direction, for
bodies whose transverse inertia tensor is degenerate or whose third moment
vanishes, and for assemblies of parts in mixed orientations, where no single
frame canonicalizes every component. ISLA needs neither a frame estimate nor
a global direction at inference; there the contract is the difference
between a working surrogate and the first row of @tbl-pose. Against
baselines that learn pose from augmentation rather than from a canonical
frame, the contract also earns accuracy (@sec-scoreboard-pose).
:::

## Learning-rate sensitivity is part of the protocol {#sec-lr-protocol}

**The architectures lose very different amounts of accuracy at a wrong
learning rate, so a protocol sharing one rate would measure tuning luck
instead of architecture.** One grid step above its best rate,
GeoTransolver's seed-mean error grows 9.0x on DrivAerML and 6.5x on
HiLiftAeroML; the table in the note below computes each factor from its
artifact. ISLA's side of the grid was measured on the legacy centred variant
(1.1x and 1.14x); the reference configuration's grid is being re-measured
(@sec-nb-refprops-prereg), and the point here is procedural: each
architecture runs at its own best rate. The grids are plotted as a
robustness result in @sec-robustness-lr (@fig-lr-robustness).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The learning-rate grids behind the rule (ISLA rows: legacy centred variant, diagnostic)"}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-lr-sensitivity
#| output: asis
SW = RES / "mixedres_training_2026-07-31" / "sweep"
iw = J("instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json")
round3 = json.load(open(SW / "round3_reduction.json"))
mt2_const = json.load(open(SW / "mt2_v3c_reduction.json"))
mega = json.load(open(SW / "mega_reduction.json"))
hl = J("highlift_wave_reduction.json")
dr = {"gt": {}, "isla": {}}
for arch, key in (("gt", "gt"), ("isla", "mt2")):
    for lr_key, lr in (("lr1e3", 1e-3), ("lr1e2", 1e-2)):
        dr[arch][lr] = [iw[f"iw_{key}_{lr_key}_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
dr["gt"][3e-3] = [round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["sweep_metrics"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
dr["isla"][3e-3] = ([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
                    + [mega[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (45, 46)])
hlg = {"gt": {1e-3: [hl[f"gt_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)], 3e-3: [hl[f"gt_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]},
       "isla": {1e-3: [hl[f"mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)], 3e-3: [hl[f"mt2_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]}}
name = {"gt": "GeoTransolver", "isla": "ISLA, legacy centred variant (diagnostic)"}
out = "| dataset | architecture | best rate (error) | one grid step above (error) | degradation |\n|---|---|---|---|---:|\n"
for ds, grid, steps in (("DrivAerML, 435 cars", dr, [1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2]), ("HiLiftAeroML, 1,260 cases", hlg, [1e-3, 3e-3])):
    for arch in ("gt", "isla"):
        m = {lr: mean(grid[arch][lr]) for lr in steps}
        best = min(m, key=m.get); above = steps[min(steps.index(best) + 1, len(steps) - 1)]
        f = lambda lr: f"{lr:.0e}".replace("e-0", "e-")
        if above == best:
            out += f"| {ds} | {name[arch]} | {f(best)} ({m[best]:.4f}) | none run above | — |\n"; continue
        out += f"| {ds} | {name[arch]} | {f(best)} ({m[best]:.4f}) | {f(above)} ({m[above]:.4f}) | {m[above]/m[best]:.2f}x |\n"
print(out)
print(": Learning-rate sensitivity on the full splits: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure, seed means, "
      "scored in bfloat16 (labelled: these grids predate the float32 instrument and are used only for "
      "within-architecture degradation factors), 500 epochs, 10,000 cells; DrivAerML grid {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2}, "
      "HiLiftAeroML grid {1e-3, 3e-3}. The HiLiftAeroML grid fed GeoTransolver the physical velocity, so its "
      "degradation there is a physical-velocity measurement. How to read this: the ratio in the last column is the "
      "price of one wrong grid step, within one architecture; it is not a comparison between architectures. Data: "
      "results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json, results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/"
      "{round3_reduction,mt2_v3c_reduction,mega_reduction}.json, results/highlift_wave_reduction.json. {#tbl-lr-sensitivity}")
```

:::

Two consequences are built into the protocol. Because GeoTransolver's best
rate differs between datasets, "best rate per architecture, chosen on the
full split" is the only rule under which the baseline is the strongest
version of itself on both; the rate choice moves GeoTransolver's DrivAerML
error by a few percent and does not decide the comparison (@sec-full-data).
And the rate is chosen once and frozen for every smaller split: retuning at
35 or 210 training cases would hand the baseline a search that ISLA did not
get. Rate, training-length and seed controls at the small splits move
GeoTransolver's error by far less than its input-scale sensitivity
(@tbl-unit-vs-physical), which is why the input scale is fixed by rule and
not tested by control.
